title: Reimagining Digital Well-Being and AI: A Conversation with Dr. Paul Leonardi
summary: How AI can reduce—or worsen—digital exhaustion, and what organizations can do to protect focus, reset response norms, and design sustainable work
body_markdown:
*By Dr. Paul Leonardi, Allie Blaising, Angela Ju, and Jennifer Brett*


Digital tools were meant to make work easier. Yet for many people, the always-on flow of messages, meetings, notifications, and new platforms has created a different reality: work that feels increasingly fragmented, cognitively demanding, and difficult to step away from.


Dr. Paul Leonardi, Duca Family Professor of Technology Management at UC Santa Barbara, calls this[digital exhaustion](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/760833/digital-exhaustion-by-paul-leonardi/) —the cumulative cognitive and emotional depletion that comes from using digital tools. Drawing on two decades of research across industries and roles, Leonardi finds that digital exhaustion has risen substantially. Crucially, it is not simply an individual problem of screen time, resilience, or self-discipline. It is often the result of systems: how teams set expectations for responsiveness, how organizations introduce new tools, and how work is designed and coordinated.


AI adds a new dimension to that challenge. It can reduce repetitive work, help people prepare and communicate more effectively, and create new possibilities for collaboration. But when organizations focus only on individual efficiency, AI can also shift review, correction, and coordination work onto others—creating new forms of friction and exhaustion across teams.


Upwork teams recently spoke with Dr. Leonardi as part of Reimagining Work, Upwork’s lecture series designed to provide a forum for expert practitioners and academics to exchange perspectives on the present and future of work. In the conversation, he shares what his research reveals about the systems driving digital exhaustion—and what organizations can do to protect focus, reset norms around responsiveness, and design AI-enabled work that is more sustainable rather than simply faster.


**Allie: In your research, you find that digital exhaustion has risen substantially over the past two decades. Where have organizations gone wrong in assuming exhaustion is an individual problem to manage, rather than a systems problem to design for?**


Organizations have long treated employees’ attention as if it were an unlimited resource. They add another platform, another dashboard, another communication channel, and assume people will absorb all the additional demands. When employees become exhausted from all this technology and the demands it brings, the response is often to offer time-management training or encourage them to disconnect.


But an employee can’t stop checking a tool their manager uses to assign work. And turning off notifications doesn’t remove the worry that someone is waiting for an answer from them.


My research identifies three reinforcing sources of digital exhaustion: fragmented attention, the effort of interpreting incomplete digital cues, and the emotions those interactions generate. Unless we deal directly with these sources, we’re going to exhaust our employees and stymie their productivity and passion for their work.


Individual habits of technology use can help address some of these sources for sure, but managers have to change the conditions in which those habits operate. Otherwise, we’re asking employees to solve a problem while continuing to build the environment that produces it.


**Angela: In what ways can AI both help and hurt digital exhaustion? What should that mean for how organizations set norms around AI use and redesign the work within roles?**


AI can help when it removes work that consumes attention without contributing much value. It can help people find relevant information, handle repetitive tasks, or get started on something that would otherwise require moving among several tools.


But making work faster for one person can create more work for everyone else. If AI helps me produce five documents instead of one, somebody still has to read, evaluate, and respond to them. Checking the output also requires effort. Those demands can disappear from the productivity calculation even though people still experience them.


So I’d ask managers to examine the whole workflow. What work will go away? Who will review the output? Who remains responsible when something is wrong? What happens to the time saved?


Also, I’ve found it very useful to introduce AI as something the team will learn about together, rather than a promise employees must make come true. Give people permission to say where it helps and where it creates additional work. That information should drive the redesign of their roles.


**Allie: You argue that because focus needs social permission, organizations have to architect the conditions for it. What does that look like in practice, and which practices have you found most effective in your research?**


Imagine blocking an hour to concentrate while everyone around you continues sending messages and expecting replies. You may have silenced your notifications, but you’re still thinking about what you’re missing and how your silence looks to your colleagues. That anticipation can be exhausting, too!


The practices I emphasize make focus a legitimate part of how the team works. Establish shared periods when replies are not expected. Agree on a separate route for genuinely urgent issues. Decide which conversations belong in which channels, and move an ambiguous or emotionally charged exchange to a conversation rather than extending the email thread.


Managers also have to follow those agreements themselves. A leader who praises instant replies while telling people to protect their attention sends a pretty clear message about which behavior counts.


That doesn’t mean everyone has to do the same thing; there is still room for individual differences. Some people prefer batching messages (responding to a bunch of them at once); others find regular checking reassuring (what I call streaming). Both approaches can work if they match people’s needs, goals, and personalities. The goal is to create enough shared predictability that people can choose a workable rhythm without risking their standing on the team.


**Jennifer: Many of us equate responsiveness with reliability, yet research finds that we overestimate how quickly others expect a reply. Why is it so hard to let go of being ‘always on,’ and what helps?**


A quick reply is a very visible way to show that we’re engaged. Much of our actual work is hard for other people to see because we do it on our computers in some degree of isolation from others. So we start using responsiveness to signal that we’re competent, committed, and dependable.


The trouble is that we’re often responding to expectations we’ve inferred rather than expectations anyone has stated. A late-night message arrives, and we begin wondering what the sender will think if we wait until morning. That interpretive work adds to the burden of answering the message itself.


What helps is making expectations explicit. Telling someone, “I need this by Thursday” provides useful information. So does putting in a subject line: “No response needed.” Teams should agree on what requires an immediate response and how that urgency will be communicated.


Managers need to reinforce those agreements through their behavior. Reliability should mean doing what you said you would do, when you said you would do it. People need evidence that a thoughtful response delivered at the agreed time is valued more than an immediate, incomplete one.


**Allie: If every company tracked one well-being metric as closely as it tracks productivity, what should it be and why?**


I would track digital exhaustion directly. Ask people, consistently: “How much do the digital technologies you use make you feel worn out?” That’s what I do. I use a 6-point scale. 0 means they don’t experience any exhaustion from their technologies, 6 means they are spent.


I’ve found that this question gets at something that measures of screen time, logins, or message volume can miss. Two people can spend similar amounts of time using technology and have very different experiences of it.


The value of asking this question comes from asking repeatedly and paying attention to what changes. Does exhaustion increase after a new tool is introduced? Does it fall when a team clarifies response expectations or eliminates a redundant channel? Look for patterns across teams while protecting individual privacy.


I would use the measure to investigate working conditions, not to evaluate employees’ resilience. Don’t make that mistake! A rising score should prompt a conversation about what people are being asked to monitor, interpret, and manage. Otherwise, even a well-being metric can become one more way employees feel watched.


**Allie, Angela, and Jennifer: What’s one question you’re most excited to explore over the next year at the intersection of AI, work, and well-being?**


I’m especially interested in when AI actually gives people more capacity to think, and when it simply raises expectations about how much they should produce.


That connects with my emerging work on how people invoke AI capabilities through language. People can work with the same system and elicit very different kinds of assistance. I want to understand which interactions help people exercise judgment, develop understanding, and retain control over their work, and which leave them spending more time generating and checking material.


But we also have to understand what happens around those interactions. If someone saves an hour, does that create room for deeper thinking and learning? Or does the organization immediately fill that hour with additional demands?


We need to connect what happens between a person and an AI system to how work is organized across a team. Otherwise, we can demonstrate that individual tasks get faster without knowing whether working life gets any better.


‍


[Paul Leonardi](https://paulleonardi.com/) is a leading expert on digital transformation, the future of work, and organizational networks. For more than 20 years, he has advised Fortune 500 companies, startups, and nonprofits on building smarter communication practices, fostering innovation, and managing the people side of technological change. His research and insights have appeared in *Harvard Business Review* , *MIT Sloan Management Review* , *The New York Times* , and *The Wall Street Journal* . He is the co-author of *The Digital Mindset* , which offers practical guidance for navigating a technology-driven economy, and the author of *Digital Exhaustion* , which examines how people can develop healthier, more productive relationships with digital tools. At UC Santa Barbara, Leonardi chairs the Department of Technology Management, holds the Duca Family Endowed Chair, and founded the Master of Technology Management program.


[Allie Blaising](https://www.linkedin.com/in/allie-blaising-ms) is a Senior Lead User Experience Researcher at Upwork, where she leads customer research that shapes business decisions across Upwork, with a recent focus on Small Business Growth and AI product initiatives. She holds a Master’s in Science from University of Pennsylvania.


[Angela Ju](https://www.linkedin.com/in/angela-ju-33004a1b/) **** is Senior Lead, Culture and Engagement at Upwork, where she leads team member listening programs that turn workforce insights into focused action and help leaders build adaptable teams equipped to thrive in an AI-augmented world. Prior to Upwork, Angela helped shape DEI strategy at Atlassian, ServiceNow, and Dropbox, aligning equity initiatives with business impact. With a background in communications, Angela is passionate about harnessing the power of storytelling in pursuit of a more empathetic and just world.


[Jennifer Brett](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jennifermbrett/) **** is the managing director of The Upwork Research Institute, where she leads research and thought leadership on the future of work, including AI, flexible talent, and evolving workforce models. She is a research and insights leader with more than 15 years of experience translating data, market signals, and human behavior into strategies, narratives, and business impact. Jennifer has held senior insights leadership roles at Attentive and LinkedIn across the U.S. and Europe, and previously served as an industry analyst at Google. She holds a Ph.D. in political science from Trinity College Dublin, with academic training in research design and quantitative and qualitative methods.
